description: A perennial wildflower with three broad leaves and a single nodding maroon flower. The flower has an unpleasant odor, earning it the nickname 'Stinking Benjamin.'
catskillsNotes: Abundant in higher elevation forests. One of the first spring wildflowers to emerge.

identification.leafShape: Three broad ovate leaves in whorl, 3-7" long, sessile, parallel-veined
identification.flowerDescription: Single nodding maroon-red flower, 1-2", 3 petals, strong carrion odor
identification.distinguishingFeatures: FOUL ODOR (rotting meat), nodding flower beneath leaves, maroon color
identification.lookalikeDifferences: White: white above leaves, no odor. Painted: pink V-marks. Nodding: recurved pedicel

description: Large white three-petaled flowers emerge in spring. Flowers turn pink as they age. A classic spring ephemeral of northeastern forests.
catskillsNotes: Carpets the forest floor in late April and May.

identification.leafShape: Three broad ovate leaves, 2.5-6", bluish-green, prominent veins
identification.flowerDescription: Large white flower ABOVE leaves, 1.5-3", aging to pink
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Largest trillium, white aging to pink, held ABOVE leaves
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Red: maroon, nodding, odor. Painted: pink V-marks, acidic soil

description: Pure white flowers with 8-12 petals emerge before leaves unfurl. The rhizome produces red-orange sap, giving the plant its common name.
catskillsNotes: Important early nectar source. Native Americans used the sap as dye.

identification.leafShape: Single palmately lobed leaf, 3-7 lobes, 4-9" wide, emerges wrapped around flower
identification.flowerDescription: Single white flower, 1-2", 8-12 petals, golden stamens, lasts 1-2 days
identification.distinguishingFeatures: RED-ORANGE SAP in roots (diagnostic!), wrapped emergence, earliest bloomer
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Anemones: multiple flowers, different leaves, later, WHITE sap

description: Umbrella-like leaves hide a single white nodding flower. Produces a lemon-scented fruit in late summer. Most parts of the plant are toxic.
catskillsNotes: Forms dense colonies. Fruit is edible when fully ripe but exercise caution.

identification.leafShape: 1-2 umbrella leaves, 5-9 lobes, 8-12" wide. Two leaves = flowering
identification.flowerDescription: White waxy nodding flower hidden beneath leaves, 1.5-2", sweet scent
identification.fruitSeed: Lemon-shaped yellow berry, 1-2". WARNING: Only ripe fruit edible—rest TOXIC!
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Umbrella leaves, hidden flower, colonies. TOXIC except ripe fruit!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Unique umbrella form, no lookalikes

description: One of the earliest spring blooms, with flowers in white, pink, or purple. Three-lobed leaves persist through winter.
catskillsNotes: Watch for these under fallen leaves in March.

identification.leafShape: 3-lobed evergreen leaves with SHARP-POINTED lobes, 1-3", purple-tinged beneath
identification.flowerDescription: Delicate flowers, 0.5-1", variable colors (white/pink/purple/blue), 6-10 sepals
identification.distinguishingFeatures: EARLIEST bloomer (with snow!), sharp lobes, old leaves persist
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Round-lobed has ROUNDED (not pointed) lobes

description: Distinctive hooded spathe (the 'pulpit') shelters the spadix ('Jack'). Produces bright red berries in fall.
catskillsNotes: The corm contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause burning if eaten raw.

identification.leafShape: 1-2 leaves, each with 3 large leaflets, 3-8" long, smooth margins
identification.flowerDescription: Hooded spathe (pulpit), green/purple-striped, 2-6" tall, arches over spadix (Jack)
identification.fruitSeed: Cluster of bright red berries on spadix in fall. TOXIC RAW—calcium oxalate crystals!
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Unmistakable 'preacher in pulpit' form, striped spathe. WARNING: causes burning if eaten
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Green Dragon: 5-15 leaflets (vs 3), long whip-like spadix

description: Nodding red and yellow flowers with distinctive spurred petals. A favorite of hummingbirds.
catskillsNotes: Thrives on rocky outcrops. Look for them along cliff faces and rocky trails.

identification.leafShape: Compound leaves, groups of 3 rounded lobed leaflets, fern-like, blue-green
identification.flowerDescription: Nodding red/yellow flowers, 1-2" long, 5 red spurred petals, yellow interior
identification.fruitSeed: Erect brown capsules with 5 beaked sections, black seeds
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Red/yellow bicolored nodding flowers with long spurs, grows on cliffs, hummingbird favorite
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Wild: red/yellow. Garden: blue/purple/white, different spurs

description: White flowers with yellow centers and purple-tinged backs. Grows taller than most violets, up to 16 inches.
catskillsNotes: One of the most common woodland violets in the Catskills.

identification.leafShape: Heart-shaped, toothed, 1-4" wide, on long petioles
identification.flowerDescription: White flowers, yellow center, purple-tinged back, 5 petals with purple veins, 0.5-0.75"
identification.fruitSeed: Capsules that explosively dehisce, shooting seeds several feet
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Taller than most violets (8-16"), white with yellow eye and purple back, leafy stems (not basal), blooms all summer
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Canada much taller (8-16" vs 3-5"), leafy stems vs basal, purple-tinged backs

description: Delicate white flowers shaped like upside-down pantaloons. Fern-like blue-green foliage.
catskillsNotes: Spring ephemeral. Dies back completely by summer.

identification.leafShape: Finely divided fern-like gray-green leaves, twice compound, basal
identification.flowerDescription: White/pale pink flowers shaped like upside-down pantaloons, 0.5-0.75", arching raceme of 4-10, yellow tips
identification.fruitSeed: Small capsule, black seeds with white fleshy appendages for ant dispersal
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Unmistakable 'pantaloons' shape, fern-like foliage, spring ephemeral (gone by summer), often with Squirrel Corn
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Squirrel Corn: heart-shaped (not pantaloon) flowers, fragrant, yellow tubers like corn

whereToLook: Rich woods with deep leaf mold

description: Large pink pouch-shaped flower rises between two basal leaves. A wild orchid requiring specific mycorrhizal fungi.
catskillsNotes: Protected species. Never pick or transplant. Requires decades to reach flowering maturity.

identification.leafShape: Two large basal leaves, broadly elliptic, 4-8" long, deeply pleated with parallel veins, NO stem leaves
identification.flowerDescription: Single large pink pouch-shaped flower (slipper), 1.5-2" long, veined with deeper pink, twisted brown-purple sepals/petals
identification.fruitSeed: Capsule with thousands of dust-like seeds requiring specific fungi
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Large pink inflated pouch, ONLY 2 basal leaves, requires mycorrhizal fungi, takes 10-17 years to bloom. PROTECTED—never pick/transplant!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Pink has 2 basal leaves (others leafy stems), pink pouch no white, acidic soil (others calcium-rich)

description: Striking bicolored orchid with purple hood and white lip. Sweet-scented flowers attract early pollinators.
catskillsNotes: One of the earliest orchids to bloom. Becoming less common due to habitat loss.

identification.leafShape: Two large basal leaves, broadly elliptic, 3-8" long, glossy, deeply ribbed
identification.flowerDescription: Spike of 3-8 showy bicolored flowers, purple hood with white lip, 0.5-1", sweet-scented
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Striking bicolored orchid (purple/white), sweet scent, early bloomer, only 2 basal leaves
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Showy Orchis: bicolored purple/white flowers in spike. Lady's Slipper: single pink pouch flower

peakSeason: Late April-May, one of earliest orchids

description: Nodding yellow lily-like flowers. Mottled leaves resemble brook trout markings. Forms extensive colonies.
catskillsNotes: Only plants with two leaves produce flowers. Can take 7 years to bloom.

identification.leafShape: 1-2 mottled leaves, elliptic, 3-8" long, brown/green marbling resembles trout, basal. ONLY 2-leaf plants flower!
identification.flowerDescription: Single nodding yellow lily-like flower, 1-1.5", 6 recurved tepals, brownish outside
identification.fruitSeed: Capsule with seeds having elaiosomes for ant dispersal
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Mottled trout-pattern leaves (diagnostic!), nodding yellow flower, forms huge colonies (takes 7+ years to flower)
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No similar species—mottled leaves are unique

description: Arching stem with plume of creamy white flowers at the tip. Produces speckled red berries in fall.
catskillsNotes: Young shoots edible like asparagus. Berries were used by indigenous peoples.

identification.leafShape: Alternate leaves, broadly lance-shaped, 3-6" long, parallel-veined, arching stem
identification.flowerDescription: Plume of creamy-white flowers at stem tip, feathery panicle, sweet-scented
identification.fruitSeed: Speckled red berries (green with red spots, then fully red), in terminal cluster
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Arching zigzag stem, flowers at TIP (vs along stem), feathery plume, red berries in fall
identification.lookalikeDifferences: False: flowers at tip, plume-like. True: flowers dangle along stem in pairs, tubular

description: Pairs of white-green tubular flowers dangle beneath arching stems. Blue-black berries in fall.
catskillsNotes: Rhizome scars resemble official seals, giving the plant its name.

identification.leafShape: Alternate leaves, ovate, 2-6" long, parallel-veined, on arching stem
identification.flowerDescription: Pairs of white-green tubular flowers dangling BENEATH stem from leaf axils, 0.5-1"
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Arching stem, flowers in PAIRS dangling along stem (not at tip), tubular bells, rhizome scars resemble seals
identification.lookalikeDifferences: True: paired tubular flowers along stem. False: plume of flowers at tip only

description: Rose-purple five-petaled flowers. Deeply lobed leaves. Seed capsules explode when ripe.
catskillsNotes: Root was used medicinally by settlers and Native Americans.

identification.leafShape: Deeply palmately lobed basal leaves, 3-5 lobes, toothed margins, long petioles
identification.flowerDescription: Rose-purple 5-petaled flowers, 1-1.5 inches across, in loose clusters
identification.fruitSeed: Capsules with long beak that explosively dehisces, catapulting seeds
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Purple flowers, deeply lobed palmate leaves, explosive seed dispersal, sticky hairs
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Wild Geranium is larger, deeper purple, native woodland plant

description: Spikes of tiny white flowers create a foam-like appearance. Heart-shaped leaves with bronze markings.
catskillsNotes: Spreads by stolons, forming attractive groundcover in shaded areas.

identification.leafShape: Heart-shaped basal leaves, 2-4 inches wide, lobed and toothed, with bronze markings, semi-evergreen
identification.flowerDescription: Spikes of tiny white flowers creating feathery foam-like appearance, 3-6 inch spike
identification.distinguishingFeatures: White foamy flower spikes, heart-shaped leaves with bronze markings, spreads by stolons
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Foamflower has feathery flowers and is larger; Miterwort has fringed flowers

description: Hidden maroon flowers at ground level beneath heart-shaped leaves. Rhizomes have ginger-like aroma.
catskillsNotes: Flowers are pollinated by fungus gnats and ground beetles.

identification.leafShape: Two large heart-shaped leaves, 3-6 inches wide, velvety-hairy, kidney-shaped, hide flower
identification.flowerDescription: Hidden maroon cup-shaped flower AT GROUND LEVEL beneath leaves, 3-lobed, 1 inch, hairy
identification.distinguishingFeatures: HIDDEN flower at ground level (must lift leaves to see!), ginger-scented rhizome when broken
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No lookalikes - unique hidden flower and ginger scent make ID certain

whereToLook: Shaded slopes in deep leaf litter

description: Delicate white to pink flowers on thin stems. Compound leaves resembling meadow-rue.
catskillsNotes: Also called Rue Anemone. Blooms for several weeks in spring.

identification.leafShape: Compound leaves divided into 3 delicate leaflets resembling meadow-rue, fern-like appearance
identification.flowerDescription: White to pale pink flowers, 0.5-1 inch across, 5-10 petal-like sepals, on thin stems
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Delicate Rue Anemone, compound meadow-rue-like leaves, blooms for several weeks
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Wood/Rue Anemone very similar. Canada Anemone is much larger with different leaf structure

description: Small white to pink flowers with darker pink veining. Narrow grass-like leaves. Edible corms.
catskillsNotes: Can form carpets of flowers in suitable habitat. An important early nectar source.

identification.leafShape: Two narrow grass-like succulent leaves per stem, 2-6 inches long
identification.flowerDescription: Small white to pale pink flowers with darker pink veining, 5 petals, 0.5 inch, in clusters
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Grass-like narrow leaves, pink-veined white flowers, edible corms, can form carpets
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No dangerous lookalikes; corms are edible and nutritious

description: Greenish-yellow flowers appear before leaves fully expand. Blue berry-like seeds in fall.
catskillsNotes: Historically used medicinally, but contains toxic compounds. Handle with care.

identification.leafShape: Large compound leaves, 2-3 times divided, blue-green and glaucous (waxy coating)
identification.flowerDescription: Greenish-yellow to purplish small flowers appearing before leaves fully expand, 6-petaled, in clusters
identification.fruitSeed: Bright BLUE berry-like seeds on thick stalks (not true berries). WARNING: TOXIC!
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Blue-green glaucous leaves, flowers before full leaf expansion, distinctive TOXIC blue 'berries' in fall
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Blue Cohosh has blue seeds and compound leaves; Black Cohosh has white flower spikes and different foliage

peakSeason: April-May for flowers, August-September for blue seeds

description: Tiny white flowers on thread-like stems. Evergreen three-parted leaves. Named for golden-yellow roots.
catskillsNotes: Prefers cool, moist habitats at higher elevations. Used historically for canker sores.

identification.leafShape: Evergreen compound leaves divided into 3 shiny dark green leaflets, persistent year-round
identification.flowerDescription: Tiny white flowers on thread-like stems, 0.25-0.5 inch across, solitary, 5-7 petal-like sepals
identification.distinguishingFeatures: GOLDEN-YELLOW THREADLIKE ROOTS (diagnostic - gently pull plant to see!), evergreen leaves, prefers cool mossy sites
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Goldthread has 3-parted evergreen leaves, golden roots, and grows in cool bogs; Rue Anemone is deciduous

description: White petals with magenta V-shaped markings at the base. Prefers cooler, more acidic soils than other trilliums.
catskillsNotes: More common at higher elevations. Indicator of undisturbed forest.

identification.leafShape: Three ovate leaves in whorl, 2-5 inches long, on short petioles (unlike other trilliums), bluish-green
identification.flowerDescription: White petals with distinctive MAGENTA V-SHAPED MARKINGS at base, 2-3 inches across, held erect above leaves
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Diagnostic PINK/MAGENTA V-MARKS at petal base! Prefers cool acidic soils, indicator of undisturbed forest
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Painted has magenta V-marks and prefers acidic soil; White is pure white on neutral soil; Red is maroon

peakSeason: May-June, blooms later than other trilliums

description: Low-growing dogwood with white 'flower' (actually bracts). Produces clusters of red berries in fall.
catskillsNotes: Found primarily in higher, cooler elevations. Berries are edible but bland.

identification.leafShape: Whorl of 4-6 oval leaves at stem top, 1-3 inches long, parallel-veined, resembles tiny dogwood
identification.flowerDescription: White 'flower' (actually 4 white bracts surrounding tiny greenish true flowers), 1 inch across
identification.fruitSeed: Cluster of bright red berries in a bunch (gives name Bunchberry). Edible but bland
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Miniature dogwood appearance, 4 white bracts, low creeping habit forming carpets, distinctive red berry cluster
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Bunchberry is low creeping herb; Flowering dogwood is a tree. Both have similar bract structure

description: Yellow bell-shaped flowers on leafless stalks. Produces bright blue berries. Large glossy leaves.
catskillsNotes: Also called Corn Lily. Berries are toxic despite attractive appearance.

identification.leafShape: 2-5 large glossy basal leaves, broadly lance-shaped, 5-12 inches long, parallel-veined, NO stem leaves
identification.flowerDescription: Yellow bell-shaped flowers, nodding, 3-8 flowers on single leafless stalk
identification.fruitSeed: Bright porcelain-BLUE berries in cluster (gives name Bluebead). Very showy but TOXIC!
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Glossy basal leaves, yellow bells on leafless stalk, bright BLUE TOXIC berries (don't eat despite beauty!)
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Clintonia has yellow bell flowers and blue berries; Avens has different flower and fruit structure

description: Distinctive tiered whorls of leaves. Small yellow flowers. Root tastes like cucumber.
catskillsNotes: Edible root but harvest threatens the plant. Better to appreciate than consume.

identification.leafShape: Distinctive TIERED WHORLS: 5-9 leaves at mid-stem, 3 leaves at top (if flowering)
identification.flowerDescription: Small yellowish-green nodding flowers from upper whorl, 3-parted, recurved
identification.distinguishingFeatures: TIERED architecture (unmistakable!), cucumber-scented root (edible but harvest threatens plant)
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No lookalikes - unique tiered whorl structure makes ID certain

description: Delicate white star-shaped flowers (usually 7 petals) on thin stems. Whorl of lance-shaped leaves.
catskillsNotes: Common in cool mountain forests. The number of petals often varies.

identification.leafShape: Whorl of 5-7 lance-shaped leaves at stem top, 1.5-3 inches long, on thin delicate stem
identification.flowerDescription: Delicate white star-shaped flowers, USUALLY 7 PETALS (can vary 5-9), on thin stalks above leaf whorl
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Count the petals - usually 7! (unique). Whorl of leaves below flowers, very delicate appearance
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No obvious lookalikes - 7-petaled star flowers and leaf whorl are distinctive

description: Shrub with flat-topped flower clusters. Large leaves turn burgundy in fall. Sprawling branches can trip hikers.
catskillsNotes: Branches root where they touch ground. Red berries turn black when ripe.

identification.leafShape: Large opposite heart-shaped leaves, 4-8 inches wide, finely toothed, prominent veins, turn burgundy/purple in fall
identification.flowerDescription: Flat-topped flower clusters with large showy sterile outer flowers (white, 1 inch) and small fertile inner flowers
identification.fruitSeed: Red berries turning black when ripe, in flat clusters
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Large heart-shaped leaves, flat flower clusters (like hydrangea), sprawling branches that root at tips and can trip hikers (gives name!)
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Hobblebush has larger leaves and sprawling habit; Maple-leaved Viburnum is more upright with smaller leaves

description: Fluffy white flower clusters. Produces clusters of bright red berries. All parts are toxic.
catskillsNotes: Also called Doll's Eyes (white form). Berries are highly poisonous.

identification.leafShape: Large compound leaves, twice divided into sharply toothed leaflets, 2-4 inches long
identification.flowerDescription: Fluffy white flower clusters, dense raceme 2-4 inches long, many stamens give fuzzy appearance
identification.fruitSeed: Bright RED berries in clusters on thick red stalks (white form called Doll's Eyes). ALL PARTS HIGHLY TOXIC!
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Fluffy white flowers, RED berries on RED stalks (or white berries on red stalks - Doll's Eyes). POISON WARNING!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Red Baneberry: red berries on red stalks. White: white berries on red stalks. Black Cohosh: different flowers, no berries

peakSeason: May-June for flowers, August-September for berries

description: White flowers with pink veining. Clover-like leaves that fold at night. Lemony-sour taste.
catskillsNotes: Leaves contain oxalic acid. Safe in small quantities but avoid excessive consumption.

identification.leafShape: Clover-like leaves with 3 heart-shaped leaflets, fold down at night and in rain, delicate
identification.flowerDescription: White flowers with pink veining, 5 petals, 0.5-0.75 inch across, nodding
identification.fruitSeed: Explosive capsules that shoot seeds when ripe or touched
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Clover leaves that FOLD AT NIGHT (nyctinastic movement), lemony-sour taste (oxalic acid), grows in cool sites
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Wood Sorrel has white/pink flowers in cool forests; Yellow has yellow flowers in sunny areas

description: Creeping evergreen with paired white flowers. Produces bright red berries that persist through winter.
catskillsNotes: Each berry is formed from two flowers. Edible but dry and tasteless.

identification.leafShape: Small evergreen opposite leaves, rounded, 0.25-0.5 inch, shiny dark green
identification.flowerDescription: Paired white tubular flowers (ALWAYS in pairs!), 4-lobed, 0.5 inch, fragrant
identification.fruitSeed: Bright red berry formed from TWO FUSED flowers (has 2 'eyes' or dots). Persists through winter. Edible but dry/tasteless
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Creeping evergreen, paired flowers (diagnostic!), berries with 2 'eyes' from flower fusion
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Partridgeberry is creeping with paired flowers and 2-eyed berries; Wintergreen is more upright with single flowers

peakSeason: June-July for flowers, berries persist through winter

description: Pink snapdragon-like flowers resembling turtle heads. Opposite leaves. Prefers wet soils.
catskillsNotes: Host plant for Baltimore Checkerspot butterfly larvae.

identification.leafShape: Opposite lance-shaped leaves, 3-6 inches long, sharply toothed
identification.flowerDescription: Pink snapdragon-like flowers resembling turtle heads, 1-1.5 inches long, in dense terminal spike
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Pink turtle-head-shaped flowers, wet habitat requirement, host for Baltimore Checkerspot butterfly
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Pink Turtlehead has pink flowers; White has white/pale pink flowers. Otherwise very similar

description: Tall lily with orange flowers that have strongly recurved petals. Dark spots. Can reach 8 feet.
catskillsNotes: Spectacular when found. Prefers wet, sunny openings.

identification.leafShape: Whorled lance-shaped leaves in tiers along stem, 3-6 inches long
identification.flowerDescription: Orange flowers with strongly RECURVED petals (rolled back), dark spots, 3-4 inches across, many flowers per stem
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Very tall (up to 8 feet!), orange flowers with STRONGLY RECURVED petals (like a turban), wet habitat
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Turk's Cap: very tall, strongly recurved petals, wet sites. Wood: shorter, upfacing, dry sites

description: Upward-facing orange-red flowers with dark spots. More compact than Turk's Cap. Prefers drier sites.
catskillsNotes: Becoming uncommon due to deer browsing and collection. Never pick.

identification.leafShape: Whorled or alternate lance-shaped leaves, 2-4 inches long
identification.flowerDescription: Orange-red UPWARD-FACING flowers with dark spots, 2-3 inches across, 1-3 flowers per stem
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Upward-facing (not nodding) orange-red flowers, shorter than Turk's Cap, dry habitat, RARE - never pick!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Wood Lily: upward-facing flowers, shorter, dry sites. Turk's Cap: recurved petals, tall, wet sites

description: Similar to sharp-lobed hepatica but with rounded leaf lobes. Flowers white, pink, blue, or purple.
catskillsNotes: Often found growing alongside sharp-lobed hepatica in mixed forests.

identification.leafShape: Three-lobed evergreen leaves with ROUNDED lobes, 1-3 inches wide, leathery, purple-tinged beneath
identification.flowerDescription: Delicate flowers on hairy stalks, 0.5-1 inch, variable colors (white/pink/blue/purple), 6-10 sepals
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Very early bloomer, ROUNDED (not pointed) leaf lobes, often grows WITH Sharp-lobed Hepatica - check lobes!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Round-lobed has ROUNDED leaf lobes; Sharp-lobed has POINTED lobes. Often grow together - leaf tips are key!

description: Nodding yellow bell-shaped flowers. Perfoliate leaves (stem appears to pierce leaves).
catskillsNotes: Young shoots edible like asparagus. Also called Merrybells.

identification.leafShape: Perfoliate leaves (stem appears to pierce through leaf), 2-4 inches long, pale green
identification.flowerDescription: Nodding yellow bell-shaped flowers, 1-1.5 inches long, twisted petals, dangles beneath leaves
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Perfoliate leaves (stem through leaf - diagnostic!), nodding yellow bells, young shoots edible like asparagus
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Bellwort has perfoliate leaves; Wild Oats has sessile (clasping) leaves

description: Clusters of pink buds open to sky-blue tubular flowers. Dies back by midsummer.
catskillsNotes: Prefers lower elevation valleys. Spring ephemeral that disappears after blooming.

identification.leafShape: Smooth oval leaves, 2-6 inches long, pale green, alternate on stem
identification.flowerDescription: Pink buds open to SKY-BLUE tubular flowers in nodding clusters, 1 inch long, 5-lobed
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Pink buds opening to sky-blue flowers (color change!), spring ephemeral (disappears by summer), prefers floodplains
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Virginia Bluebells are much larger, tubular (vs flat), and are spring ephemerals

peakSeason: April-May, completely dies back by midsummer

description: White flower nods beneath the leaves on a strongly recurved pedicel. Prefers wetter sites.
catskillsNotes: Less common than red or white trillium. Look in swampy areas.

identification.leafShape: Three ovate leaves in whorl, 2-5 inches long, petioled
identification.flowerDescription: WHITE flower on STRONGLY RECURVED pedicel that nods BENEATH leaves, 1-1.5 inches, 3 petals
identification.distinguishingFeatures: White flower on strongly recurved/bent pedicel hanging BENEATH leaves (diagnostic!), prefers wet areas
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Nodding: white flower on recurved pedicel beneath leaves. Red: maroon, odor. White: white above leaves

description: White eight-petaled flowers. Distinctive leaves split into two halves. Rare in Catskills.
catskillsNotes: Limited to limestone-rich areas. Protected in some states.

identification.leafShape: Unique leaf split into TWO HALVES (like butterfly wings), each half 2-4 inches long, on long petiole
identification.flowerDescription: White 8-petaled flower, 1 inch across, appears before leaves fully expand
identification.fruitSeed: Capsule opens like a hinged lid
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Unique TWIN-LOBED leaves (like butterfly, no other plant similar!), rare in Catskills, limestone areas only
identification.lookalikeDifferences: No lookalikes - twin-lobed leaf structure is completely unique

description: Similar to Dutchman's Breeches but flowers are more heart-shaped. Yellow tubers resemble corn kernels.
catskillsNotes: Often grows with Dutchman's Breeches. Fragrant flowers.

identification.leafShape: Finely divided fern-like gray-green leaves, twice compound, basal
identification.flowerDescription: White to pale pink HEART-SHAPED flowers (vs pantaloons), 0.5-0.75 inch, fragrant, in raceme
identification.fruitSeed: Small capsule, underground YELLOW TUBERS resembling corn kernels (give name)
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Heart-shaped flowers (not pantaloons!), fragrant (vs odorless), yellow corn-like tubers underground
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Squirrel Corn: heart-shaped fragrant flowers, yellow tubers. Dutchman's: pantaloon-shaped, not fragrant

peakSeason: April-May, often grows WITH Dutchman's Breeches

description: Broad leaves emerge in spring and die before white flower stalk appears. Strong onion-garlic odor.
catskillsNotes: Highly sought as wild food but over-harvested in many areas. Harvest sustainably.

identification.leafShape: 2-3 broad elliptic leaves, 6-12 inches long, emerge in early spring then DIE BACK before flowering
identification.flowerDescription: White flowers in umbel on leafless stalk (leaves GONE by flowering time!), late spring/summer
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Strong onion-garlic odor (diagnostic!), leaves emerge early then disappear, flowers appear on bare stalk. WARNING: Often overharvested!
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Ramps: strong garlic smell, edible. False hellebore: NO SMELL, POISONOUS! Always smell-test!

peakSeason: April-May for leaves, June-July for flowers

description: Compound leaves on separate stalks from flowers. Greenish flower clusters. Purple-black berries.
catskillsNotes: Root was used as sarsaparilla substitute. Important wildlife food.

identification.leafShape: Single large compound leaf on separate stalk from flowers, divided into 3-5 leaflets, each 2-5 inches
identification.flowerDescription: Greenish-white flowers in 2-7 round clusters (umbels) on separate stalk BELOW leaves
identification.distinguishingFeatures: Compound leaf on one stalk, flowers on separate shorter stalk (unique arrangement), aromatic roots
identification.lookalikeDifferences: Sarsaparilla: compound leaf separate from flower stalk. Ginseng: different structure, much rarer

peakSeason: May-June for flowers, August-September for berries

description: Pure white (no chlorophyll) plant that turns black when mature. Parasitic on mycorrhizal fungi.
catskillsNotes: Also called Ghost Plant or Corpse Plant. Not a fungus despite appearance.

identification.leafShape: NO GREEN LEAVES - entire plant white/translucent (no chlorophyll!)
identification.flowerDescription: Single white/pinkish nodding pipe-shaped flower at stem tip, becomes erect in fruit
identification.distinguishingFeatures: GHOSTLY WHITE (no chlorophyll!), parasitic on fungi (not a fungus!), turns BLACK when old or picked
